newsitem.title: USA: More jurors join pool for O.J. Simpson civil trial.
newsitem.headline: More jurors join pool for O.J. Simpson civil trial.

text.p: The judge in the O.J. Simpson civil trial accepted three more people into a pool of prospective jurors Tuesday, including a woman who said she had visited the scene of the murders and a man who considered the former football star "probably guilty."
Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki dismissed a man who said on a jury questionnaire that Simpson's slain ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, was a "flirt" who "deserved what she got."

Simpson, a former star running back, Hollywood actor and TV celebrity, was acquitted in October, 1995, of murdering Brown and her friend Ronald Goldman. The two were found slashed to death outside her Los Angeles home June 12, 1994.

The families of the victims have filed a wrongful-death civil suit alleging Simpson was liable for the deaths. If they prevail in the civil trial, Simpson could face paying millions of dollars in damages.

Fujisaki and the lawyers in the case questioned eight more potential jurors before the lunch break Tuesday, retaining two white men and a black woman. The judge excused three black women, a white man and an Asian man.

As of mid-day Tuesday, the start of the fourth week of jury selection, Fujisaki had built a pool of 91 prospective jurors. He wants about 100 before starting the final phase of examination that will eventually yield 12 jurors and eight alternates.

Among the people questioned Tuesday were a black woman who said she had visited Nicole Brown's condominium, the scene of the double murders, but who said she had little opinion about the case or the criminal trial verdict.
The woman said she simply had driven by the scene at the request of her cousins, but "if they (the cousins) asked me I would tell them I didn't have an opinion."
She also said that she stayed at her desk at work during the verdict, while 200 of her fellow employees gathered in the next room to watch it on television.
"About half of the people were screaming 'no' and half were screaming 'yes,'" she said. But "everybody in my job already knew I wasn't interested in the case."
A white man said he did not follow the case much, but that from what he had seen Simpson was probably guilty of the crimes and not the victim of a police frame-up as defence lawyers had claimed.
Simpson's attorneys asked Fujisaki to excuse the man, but the judge refused. Simpson himself was not in court.
In other developments Tuesday, Simpson's friend and sometime lawyer Robert Kardashian said in a taped television interview that he has begun to doubt Simpson's innocence.
"I have doubts. The blood evidence is the biggest thorn in my side," he told ABC's programme 20/20.
